description: Data Scientist and BI Analyst and Quality Analyst from Costa Rica working on the MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. Skills: Python, machine learning (scikit-learn, XGBoost), Tableau and Power BI. Not recruiting for now, but happy to connect with other participants.
summary: Data Masters turns 25 years of NASA FIRMS hot spot detections into one comparable record for any country on Earth. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) count heat differently: VIIRS reports about 4.5 times more detections, so merging the records as they are creates a false jump in 2012 and an error of about 80 % per country and year. We harmonize MODIS into VIIRS-equivalent detections with a machine learning model per FIRMS hot spot type (vegetation fires, gas flaring and industry, volcanoes, offshore), with a typical error of 5.5 % per country and year on held-out years. Our web app answers one question: is this week or month normal here? It offers a burn calendar from 2000 to today, comparison with the historical median, weekly and monthly alerts, a ranking of countries above normal and near-real-time VIIRS detections. This matters because landscape-fire smoke is linked to about 1.5 million deaths a year (The Lancet, 2024) and MODIS shuts down in 2027. With one long, comparable record, governments, aid agencies and fire services can spot an unusual season early and move funding, masks and crews in time.
details:
We are Kevin and Dana, a team from Costa Rica. By the end of May this year our country already had 233 wildfires and more than 30,000 hectares burned, and every dry season firefighters and health officials ask the same question: is this normal, or worse than usual? NASA satellites have recorded hot spots around the world since 2000, but the record comes from two sensors that don't count fire the same way. VIIRS, which started in 2012, sees about 4.5 times more than MODIS, so if you join them as they are, fires seem to explode in 2012 and the numbers are off by around 80%.

Data Masters fixes that and gives every country one 25-year history built from NASA FIRMS data. You click a country on the globe and right away you see whether this week or month is above normal, and by how much. When we tested it with the United States, it flagged seven weeks in a row above normal starting on August 17, 2020, about four times the usual level, right when the record western fire season began. The app also ranks the countries above normal each month, has a burn calendar back to 2000, shows the latest VIIRS detections and lets you download reports and data.

To connect the two sensors we trained a LightGBM model on 0.5 degree cells, using what Terra and Aqua saw by day and night, fire intensity, nearby cells and months, the position of the Sun, and the place and date. We decided early that it couldn't be only about wildfires, so gas flares, volcanoes and offshore platforms each have their own model. We only trusted results on years the model had never seen, and the error per country and year dropped from about 80% to 5.5%. It works well in 130 of 149 countries, and the app shows the other 19 instead of hiding them.

This matters because smoke from landscape fires is linked to around 1.5 million deaths a year, mostly in poorer countries. An early warning gives people time: clinics and schools can prepare, fire crews can move before the worst weeks, and governments and aid agencies can send money, masks and equipment where they will be needed. It also helps track gas flaring, which burned 151 billion cubic meters in 2024. Suomi NPP already stopped sending data and MODIS ends in 2027, so this is the moment to save the record. We built it in Python with Streamlit, DuckDB, pandas and Plotly, and it is free, open source and available in English and Spanish.
